title: The score card with no evidence
scenario:
You work in the strategy team of a mid-size online bank. A colleague scored three AI candidates for next quarter and wants the steering group to approve the top one. Before the meeting, your manager asks you to check the score card.

The exhibit shows the card and the colleague's notes.
exhibit:
AI candidates, scored 1-3 (made-up example data)

                         Value  Fit  Success  Risk*  Ready  Total
A. Sort incoming customer  3     3      3       3      3     15
   messages by topic
B. Approve or reject       3     3      1       1      2     10
   small-business loans
C. Draft answers to        2     3      2       2      1     10
   questions about a
   savings product that
   launches next month

* Risk: 3 = mistakes are cheap and easy to fix

Notes:
A: 9,000 messages a month; 3 years of labeled messages; messages
   arrive in 5 languages; topics change each quarter.
B: Success = "good lending decisions". A wrong approval can lose
   the full loan amount.
C: Product is new, so there are no past questions yet.

questions.prompt: Why does candidate A score high on "fit"?

options.text: Because it has the highest volume, and fit is the same thing as volume in a score card.
options.explanation: Volume is scored under value. Fit asks whether the task itself suits a language model.

options.text: Because sorting messages is a simple task that any keyword rule can already do well.
options.explanation: If a keyword rule could do it, fit would be low. The notes describe free text in five languages with changing topics.

options.text: Because sorting by topic needs no testing, so it is safe to start without checks.
options.explanation: Every use case needs testing. Fit is about the kind of task, not about skipping checks.

options.text: Because the messages are free text in 5 languages, and the topics change each quarter.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's ticket routing guide lists changing categories, unstructured text and many languages as signs an LLM fits.

questions.prompt: Candidate B's success line says "good lending decisions". What is the best rewrite?

options.text: "The model should make lending decisions that are as good as possible and that customers like."
options.explanation: This is still vague. Nothing here can be measured or compared with today.

options.text: "On 500 past applications with known outcomes, agree with the final credit decision 95% of the time."
options.explanation: Right. It is specific, measurable and tied to the real task, as Anthropic's success criteria guide asks.

options.text: "The model should never make a bad lending decision under any circumstances, for any customer."
options.explanation: OpenAI's accuracy guide says LLMs are unlikely to reach 99.999% accuracy with off-the-shelf methods. A target nobody can meet isn't achievable.

options.text: "The lending team should feel that the model's decisions are good after using it for a month."
options.explanation: A feeling is not a measure. Nobody can compare it with today's results or check it again later.

questions.prompt: A wrong approval in B can lose the full loan. What does OpenAI's accuracy guide suggest for a case like this?

options.text: Drop the use case for good, because any task with a high cost of error can never use AI.
options.explanation: The guide doesn't stop at "no". In its fraud example, the AI stayed in the process as an assistant.

options.text: Let the model approve loans alone, but only on the days when the lending team is very busy.
options.explanation: The cost of a wrong approval is the same on a busy day. Full autonomy is the risky part.

options.text: Let a person lead the decision, with the AI as an assistant, for example preparing a summary.
options.explanation: Right. In the guide's fraud example, where failure was costly, the team chose a human to lead and the AI to assist.

options.text: Raise B's risk score to 3, because a better model will make mistakes too rare to matter.
options.explanation: The risk score is about what a mistake costs, and that cost doesn't change with a newer model.

questions.prompt: Candidate C scores 1 on "ready". What is the main reason?

options.text: There are no past questions with known good answers to test the model against yet.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's ticket routing guide lists a sample set of historical tickets for testing as a prerequisite. A product that hasn't launched has none.

options.text: Savings products are a regulated topic, and AI may never be used for them at a bank.
options.explanation: The notes give no such rule. The low score comes from missing test examples.

options.text: Drafting answers to questions is a poor fit for language models in general.
options.explanation: Fit is scored 3 for C. The weak point is readiness, not fit.

options.text: Its total of 10 is lower than A's total of 15, so it must also score low on readiness.
options.explanation: The total comes from the five scores, not the other way round. Readiness is low for its own reason.
